Three concrete tasks, captured in Flik 0.3.0. Every scenario includes the input files, command and visible result.

BackendDevopsKubernetes

BACKEND / INCIDENT INVESTIGATION

An API timeout. A worker retry. One view.

Bring three local service logs together and keep the source of each event visible.

Reproduce it

api.log ↓ · worker.log ↓ · auth.log ↓

flik -m api.log worker.log auth.log
  1. Download api.log, worker.log and auth.log into a new empty directory, keeping these filenames.
  2. Run the command above. These fixtures contain 60 synthetic events with interleaved timestamps.
  3. Look for upstream timeout in api.log and retry scheduled in worker.log. Follow mode continues polling the local files.

What to look for

The API reports upstream timeout at 10:00:52. The worker schedules a retry at 10:00:56. Colored source labels distinguish each service in the combined stream.

What you get

Inspect the API error and worker retry in the same view, with their filenames and timestamps preserved. Shared request text is a clue to investigate, not proof of causality.

Scope and limits

Existing events and each live polling batch are timestamp-sorted. Late arrivals stay appended. Initial inputs are loaded into memory and the temporary merged file grows; same-size or larger replacement files can miss events.

DEVOPS / LIVE LOG READING

Keep the previous pages beside the current events.

Use a wide terminal to retain more consecutive history while following a stream.

Reproduce it

api.log ↓ · worker.log ↓ · auth.log ↓

flik -m -l api.log worker.log auth.log
  1. Use the same three downloadable incident files in a wide terminal.
  2. Start with -m -l to combine the files and select the three-column layout.
  3. Read the pages from left to right. Press Tab or 4 to cycle layouts and compare the same input.

What to look for

The headings p-2, p-1 and Current mark three consecutive pages, ordered from left to right. Source colors stay visible in every column.

What you get

Keep earlier events on screen beside the current page. The columns represent consecutive history, not separate services.

Scope and limits

A wide terminal is needed for readable columns; long messages can be truncated in the visible view. This layout does not change merge ordering. View changes are saved in your Flik configuration.

KUBERNETES / STRUCTURED PAYLOADS

Read the nested payload behind a container log line.

Inspect a structured event without moving its payload into another tool.

Reproduce it

kubernetes.log ↓

flik kubernetes.log
  1. Download kubernetes.log into a new empty directory and open it with the command above.
  2. Select a record, then press uppercase J to open the JSON inspector.
  3. Read the service, request_id and payload.gateway values. Press Escape to return to the log view.

What to look for

The JSON inspector expands the selected event. The payload contains an amount, currency and nested gateway region and status fields.

What you get

Read the structured values behind a long container record before deciding which condition to investigate next.

Scope and limits

The inspector depends on a parseable structured payload. The screenshot uses the bundled synthetic Kubernetes fixture; it does not connect to a cluster or retrieve cloud logs.

Try it with your own logs

Start with the synthetic files above, then use a local file from your own workload. Log contents stay on your machine.
